blocks.text: A cadastral boundary linked a plan to field observations, title records and later surveys. In the nineteenth century, new grants, roads, reserves and subdivisions had to fit into an office record that staff could search and update. A plan was only one part of that chain: its number, annotations and index helped the next surveyor find the evidence behind the line.

blocks.text: The Department of Lands and Survey’s 1884–85 report lists 1,470 ten-chain sheets, 155 record maps and large-scale standard-survey sheets carrying Land Transfer surveys. These were working records. When a new survey altered a parcel, staff had to place it against the existing sheet, find its supporting plans and update the office copy.

blocks.text: There was no single database or query language. Plan numbers, annotations, registers and indexes connected the records, alongside staff knowledge of which sheet or book answered a particular question. Later cadastral systems inherited both the data and these habits of retrieval and correction.

blocks.text: The records varied in date, scale and survey quality. A line copied neatly onto a maintained sheet could still rest on older or less precise observations than its neighbour. Digital coordinates can make such a line easier to store and reproduce; they cannot add evidence that the original survey never collected.

blocks.text: Survey made boundaries reproducible, but a plan alone cannot explain the circumstances in which a boundary was created or whether the record captured Māori understandings of place and authority. Later systems could connect title, survey and Māori land records in a query. That technical link did not settle questions of provenance, control or appropriate use.

blocks.text: In 1848, Te Wharekorari shared knowledge of rivers, lakes, routes and place names with Walter Mantell during Crown land-acquisition work in the South Island. Associated sketches and purchase maps preserve some of that knowledge. Naming Te Wharekorari matters: the official who held or published a map can otherwise receive the credit while the person who supplied its geography disappears.
